title: Section index: Jesus in the Qur'an
description: Full index page for Jesus in the Qur'an. Insert on the /quran/ page with the Section index template.
content: عِيسَى ٱبۡنُ مَرۡيَمَ
All ninety-three verses on ʿĪsā ibn Maryam, grouped by theme and linked to the gospel passages they confirm or correct.

The Qur’an refers to ʿĪsā ibn Maryam in ninety-three verses, more than to any prophet but Mūsā, and between them they speak to nearly every part of his story: his mother and his birth, his signs, his message to Israel, the disciples and the table, his end and his raising, and the messenger he foretold. The Qur’an calls itself a guardian over the earlier scripture (5:48), and these verses are the guardian at work: they confirm the gospels where the gospels agree with them and correct the gospels where they do not. This part gathers the verses by theme, so that each can be set beside the gospel passage it bears on, and the whole compilation stands on one page in the order of the Qur’an.

The six themes follow his life. The annunciation and the birth gives the two tellings of Maryam’s story and what the Qur’an leaves out of the gospel nativities. The signs lists the miracles and the phrase the Qur’an attaches to every one of them: by God’s permission. A servant and a messenger sets out his titles, the denials, and the scene on the Day of Judgement in which he disowns what was said of him. The table from heaven is the meal the disciples asked for, with no death in it. The end of his earthly mission is 4:157, the one point of flat contradiction, with the historians’ consensus stated plainly beside it. The good news of Aḥmad is the messenger he announced, and the question of the Paraclete.

Each page gives the Qur’anic text in full, with the classical commentators, and then a “Compare” section naming the gospel passages. The position on these pages is the Islamic one and is labelled as such; where the scholarly consensus runs against it, as on the crucifixion, the page says so and does not soften it. The full text of every passage, with the compilation’s headings and footnotes, is on The Qur’an on Jesus, and the same passages stand inside the gospel where they fall in the story. What the classical commentators wrote on the verses that tell his story, eight works from al-Ṭabarī to al-Saʿdī translated in full, is on the classical commentaries.

The angels and Maryam, the palm tree, and the infant who speaks.
The bird of clay, the blind and the leper healed, the dead raised, by the permission of God.

Questions about Jesus in the Qur’an
<details class="wp-block-details is-style-faq"><summary>What does the Qur’an say about Jesus?</summary><!-- wp:paragraph -->

That he is ʿĪsā son of Maryam, the Messiah, a word from God and a spirit from Him, born of a virgin, a prophet and messenger sent to Israel with signs, who called people to worship God alone, was neither killed nor crucified but raised to God, and foretold a messenger after him. Ninety-three verses speak of him; see The Qur’an on Jesus.
<details class="wp-block-details is-style-faq"><summary>Does the Qur’an say Jesus was crucified?</summary><!-- wp:paragraph -->

No. Qur’an 4:157 says those who claimed to have killed the Messiah did not kill him and did not crucify him, but it was made to appear so to them, and God raised him to Himself. Historians hold the crucifixion to be well attested; this website states both plainly. See the end of his earthly mission.
<details class="wp-block-details is-style-faq"><summary>Is Jesus the Son of God in Islam?</summary><!-- wp:paragraph -->

No. The Qur’an calls him a servant and messenger of God and says it is not for God to take a son (19:35; 112:3). On the Day of Judgement he disowns any claim to be worshipped: he said only what he was commanded, worship God, my Lord and your Lord (5:116-117). See a servant and a messenger.
<details class="wp-block-details is-style-faq"><summary>Does the Qur’an teach the virgin birth of Jesus?</summary><!-- wp:paragraph -->

Yes. Maryam asks how she can have a child when no man has touched her, and is told that God creates what He wills (3:47; 19:20-21). The Qur’an treats the birth as a sign of God’s power, like the creation of Adam without a father (3:59), not as proof of the child’s divinity. See the annunciation and the birth.
<details class="wp-block-details is-style-faq"><summary>What miracles did Jesus perform according to the Qur’an?</summary><!-- wp:paragraph -->

He healed the blind from birth and the leper, raised the dead, made a bird from clay and breathed life into it, spoke in the cradle, told people what they had stored in their houses, and prayed down a table from heaven, each one “by God’s permission” (3:49; 5:110-115). See the signs.
<details class="wp-block-details is-style-faq"><summary>Who is Aḥmad in Qur’an 61:6?</summary><!-- wp:paragraph -->

The messenger Jesus foretold: “giving good news of a messenger who will come after me, whose name is Aḥmad.” Aḥmad, “most praised”, is from the same root as Muḥammad, and Muslims have always read the verse of him. Whether John’s Paraclete preserves the prophecy is discussed on the good news of Aḥmad.

A measure is for measuring something. The next part, The Gospel According to Islam, is the life of ʿĪsā ibn Maryam told as a gospel with the Qur’an as its measure: the gospel material that agrees with it kept, the rest set aside and named.
